name: Strategy Development and Backtesting
goal: Turn ideas into precise rules, test them honestly on historical data, and know how to tell a real edge from luck.
milestones: Write one complete strategy with entry, exit, stop, sizing and filter rules.
Backtest it on at least 100 trades of history (manually or in code).
Forward test it on paper for at least 1-2 months and compare with the backtest.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a strategy
body: A complete strategy has: a market and timeframe; a setup filter (when the strategy is allowed to trade, e.g. only above the 200 SMA); an entry trigger; an initial stop; exit rules (target, trailing stop or time exit); and position sizing.

Every strategy should have a reason it might work. Common edges come from trend persistence (momentum), mean reversion (prices returning to an average after extreme moves), volatility expansion after contraction, or behavioural patterns around events.
Simple strategies tend to be more robust than complex ones. A system with three rules that works across many markets is more trustworthy than one with fifteen rules tuned to one stock.
Example trend strategy: on daily charts, if the close is above the 50 SMA and makes a new 20-day high, buy; initial stop 2 ATR below entry; exit on a close below the 20 SMA; risk 1% per trade.
keyTakeaways: Strategy = filter + entry + stop + exit + sizing.
Know why the edge should exist.
Simple and robust beats complex and fragile.
lessons.exercise: Write the example trend strategy above into your trading plan and trade it in the simulator for 3 sessions.

lessons.title: Backtesting properly
body: A backtest applies your exact rules to historical data to see how they would have performed. It can be manual (scrolling a chart bar by bar) or automated in code.
Include realistic costs: commission, spread and slippage. Many strategies that look great without costs lose money with them, especially on short timeframes.
You need enough trades for the result to mean something: at least 100 is a common rule of thumb, across different market conditions (bull, bear, sideways).
Key output metrics: total return, max drawdown, win rate, average win/loss, profit factor, expectancy, number of trades and the Sharpe ratio (return divided by volatility).
keyTakeaways: Test exact rules, include all costs.
Look at drawdown, not only return.
lessons.exercise: Manually backtest your strategy on one stock: scroll the daily chart from 3 years ago and record 30 trades in a spreadsheet.

lessons.title: Overfitting and other traps
body: Overfitting (curve fitting) means tuning parameters until a strategy fits past noise. It looks perfect on history and fails live. Warning signs: many parameters, results that collapse if a parameter changes slightly, and very few trades.
Look-ahead bias means using information that would not have been available at the time, for example using today's close to decide to buy at today's open.
Survivorship bias means testing only on companies that still exist today, ignoring those that went bankrupt or were delisted. It makes results look better than reality.
Defences: keep an out-of-sample period you never touch while developing; use walk-forward testing; test on several markets; prefer parameters in a stable 'plateau' rather than one perfect value.
keyTakeaways: If small parameter changes destroy results, it is overfit.
Never use future information in a test.
lessons.exercise: Take any indicator setting you like (e.g. SMA 20). Test 15, 20 and 25. If results change drastically, your edge is fragile.
readMore: Marcos López de Prado, 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning'

lessons.title: From paper to live
body: After a backtest, forward test (paper trade) the strategy in real time. This tests whether you can execute it and whether the edge still exists in current markets.
Compare forward results with the backtest. Similar win rate, average R and drawdown are a good sign. A big gap means something is wrong: costs, execution or overfitting.

Go live with small size, for example a quarter of your planned risk. The goal is to experience real emotions with real money while mistakes are cheap. Increase size step by step only after a set number of trades that match expectations.
Define in advance when you will stop trading a strategy: for example if drawdown exceeds 1.5 times the worst backtest drawdown.
keyTakeaways: Backtest, then paper trade, then small live, then scale.
Compare live results to the backtest.
Pre-define when to switch a strategy off.
lessons.exercise: Write your scaling plan: how many trades at each size before increasing, and your 'switch off' drawdown.

quiz.prompt: A backtest shows 300% return with 8 trades and 12 optimised parameters. This is most likely:
options: Ready to trade with full size
quiz.explanation: Few trades plus many parameters is the classic overfitting signature.

quiz.prompt: Using the day's closing price to decide to buy at that day's open is:
quiz.explanation: You could not know the close at the open.

quiz.prompt: Testing only on today's index members ignores delisted companies. This is:
quiz.explanation: Failed companies are missing, so results look better than reality.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of out-of-sample data?
options: To test the strategy on data not used to build it
quiz.explanation: It checks whether the edge holds on unseen data.

quiz.prompt: After a good backtest and good paper trading, the next step is:
options: Go live with small size and scale up gradually
quiz.explanation: Small live trading tests execution and emotions while mistakes are cheap.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT part of a complete strategy?
quiz.explanation: No strategy guarantees profit. It defines rules and risk.
Higher Sharpe means more return per unit of risk (volatility).
